name: Bilal Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to any company, union, party or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you actually think. Sound okay?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, sounds good. I talk too much anyway, so you'll get plenty.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Great. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee drill operator at a big iron ore mine, out in the flat red country three hours from the nearest city. I drive a blasthole drill, which is a rig that bores holes in rows so the blast crew can pack them with explosives. The drill already has a GPS screen that tells me where each hole goes, and I'm still slow at levelling the rig on rough ground, so my trainer, Wen, checks my log at the end of each shift. I like the problem-solving, but twelve hours of dust and a rattling cab leave me flattened by the last hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, that's basically how it looks to me already. I use AI tools every day, and they help, but they haven't changed the dirt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the crib room, which is where we eat, that AI's handy but it's no miracle. Online I'd post something about how the hype was about selling software to bosses. People who knew me would laugh, because I'm the guy who's always showing them some new app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job's fine and I keep learning the drill. I ask a chatbot to explain the drill manual every week, and the drill still needs me to drive it. I'd still like to move up faster, because trainee pay is decent but not great, and rent in the mine town is silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the drill and aim to get my full drill ticket by mid-next year. I'd keep using the chatbot to study for it and to check my maths on hole depths. I'd keep putting about a fifth of each pay into savings, which is how I've got about four months put away now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, actually. Nothing in that picture threatens me, and I like the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent is silly. How much pressure is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a lot of my pay, but Noor, my girlfriend, teaches at the primary school, so we split it. If we were single we'd be in the camp dongas, the little portable rooms the company rents out. It's tight, not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the plateau that you'd be disappointed by?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. I was looking forward to AI making the boring paperwork easier for everyone, like the pre-start sheets we fill in by hand. Plateau means the clipboard stays.

say: AI is **handy**, but it's no miracle for mining.
The hype was mostly about **selling software** to mining bosses.
think: My **job's fine**, and the drill still needs me in the seat.
I want to **move up faster** because trainee pay doesn't stretch far.
do: Get his full **drill ticket** by the middle of next year.
Keep using a **chatbot** to study and check hole-depth maths.
Keep saving about **a fifth** of each pay.
feel: **Calm**, with a little disappointment that the paperwork stays.
S0.quote: I ask a chatbot to explain the drill manual every week, and the drill still needs me to drive it.
fieldNote: Heavy **AI user** who still sees his hands-on job as safe in this picture.
Rent is split with his **teacher girlfriend**, which keeps pressure manageable.
Mild **disappointment** that AI won't remove the clipboard paperwork.

steps.text: Get the full blasthole drill ticket by mid-next year
Use a chatbot to study and check hole-depth sums
Keep saving about a fifth of each pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I think is most likely, honestly. The mine already has a few drills that run by themselves in the north pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting, but the company has to bring the workers along, not just cut them. In the union meeting I'd ask what training they've got planned before they buy more autonomous rigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see it as a chance to jump ahead. I'd rather be the guy who knows how the robot drill thinks than the guy it replaced. The self-driving drills still need people in the control room, and people to fix the sensors, and I learn tech faster than most of the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor straight away to put me on the autonomous drill team as a trainee. I'd start a part-time online diploma in mining automation, maybe two nights a week, and pay the fees from savings. And I'd push the union to get a training deal written into the next pay agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a nervous edge. I'm not worried about me so much as the guys who hate the screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are those guys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like Wen, my trainer. He's forty-nine and the best driller on site, but he types with one finger. If the drills run themselves, his feel for the rock doesn't count for much, and that's not fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your diploma costs savings, how long until it pays off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two years. The fees are about two months of savings, so I'd be down to two months in the bank, which is lower than I like. But if I get onto the automation team, it's a step up in pay.

say: The company must **bring workers along**, not just cut them.
The union should ask about **training plans** before more autonomous rigs arrive.
think: This is a **chance to jump** ahead on the autonomous drills.
Older drillers like his **trainer** could lose out unfairly.
do: Ask to join the **autonomous drill team** as a trainee straight away.
Start a part-time **automation diploma** online, two nights a week.
Push the union for a **training deal** in the next agreement.
feel: **Excited**, with a nervous edge for colleagues who hate screens.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the guy who knows how the robot drill thinks than the guy it replaced.
fieldNote: He sees **steady disruption** as an opening, not a threat, for himself.
His concern goes to **older workers** like his trainer, whose rock sense loses value.
The diploma would cut savings to **two months**, a real risk he accepts.

steps.text: Ask the supervisor for a trainee spot on the autonomous drill team
Start a part-time online diploma in mining automation
Push the union for a training deal in the next agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's a different story. That one's not a chance to jump ahead, it's the floor falling out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say we need the government to tax the companies that use this and pay people while they retrain. I'd be posting about it, I'd be at the rally, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the control-room jobs I was aiming for go first, because they're thinking work. Then my drill job goes around 2031 when the robots catch up. Two years isn't enough time to retrain a whole mining town, and nobody's going to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the union and the town council to push for a jobs plan before 2028, not after. I'd stop the diploma, because automation control would be gone, and switch to something hands-on and people-facing, maybe paramedic training. Noor and I would cut back hard and get our savings to six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry more than scared. It feels like being handed the keys to a car that's about to be scrapped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You were excited a minute ago. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the slow one I'm faster than the machines change. In this one nobody is faster than the machines, not me, not the bosses. Being good with apps doesn't help if the app does the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Noor's teaching job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching kids feels safer, but even she's using AI to plan lessons now. If she's okay, we'd live on her wage, maybe move closer to the city where there's more work for both of us.

say: The government should **tax companies** using this and pay people to retrain.
I'd be at the **rally** and posting about it.
think: The **control-room jobs** go first, then the drill job around 2031.
Being **good with apps** doesn't help if the app does the job.
do: Push the union and **town council** for a jobs plan before 2028.
Drop the automation diploma and look at **paramedic training**.
Cut back hard and reach **six months** of savings.
feel: **Angry** more than scared, like being handed keys to a car about to be scrapped.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough time to retrain a whole mining town, and nobody's going to try.
fieldNote: His usual edge, **tech skill**, stops counting when AI outpaces everyone.
He switched quickly to a **people-facing** career idea rather than freezing.
Partner's **teaching income** is his safety net and a possible reason to move.

steps.text: Push the union and town council for a jobs plan before 2028
Switch from the automation diploma to paramedic training
Cut spending to get savings to six months
Move closer to the city where both partners can find work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking stuff, robots around 2034. That's more like a proper plan window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this well if the company and government actually start now. I'd still go to meetings, but less shouting and more planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd have time for one serious bet. Five years is long enough to finish a diploma and short enough that the mine won't wait for me. I'd still be driving the drill into my early thirties, which buys savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the drill ticket next year, then start a two-year technical diploma in electrical or maintenance in 2027. I'd keep driving to pay for it and put the rest away. I'd ask the union to get paid study days for anyone who wants them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good-ish way. Like before a big exam you've started studying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still go for automation, or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably maintenance on the machines, at least to start. Robots still break, and the first ones will need people to fix them, even if that runs out eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger brother about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lukas, my brother, is nineteen and wants to be a driller like me. I'd tell him to go for a trade that's people work, like nursing, and use the mine as a summer job.

say: There's time to do this well if they **start now**.
Union meetings should mean less shouting and more **planning** together.
think: Five years allows **one serious bet** on a new skill.
Driving the drill into his thirties **buys savings** for the switch.
do: Start a two-year **technical diploma** in maintenance in 2027.
Ask the union for **paid study days**.
feel: **Uneasy** but motivated, like before an exam he's started studying for.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to finish a diploma and short enough that the mine won't wait for me.
fieldNote: Five years turns him back into a **planner** with a single clear bet.
He'd steer his **younger brother** away from mining towards people-facing work.
He knows **maintenance work** only buys time, and says so.

steps.text: Start a two-year maintenance diploma in 2027 while still drilling
Save the rest of the drill pay towards the study years
Ask the union for paid study days for any worker

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. I'd be nearly forty, so that's half a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone being left behind with ten years' notice. If it goes badly, it's because the people at the top chose that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think about who gets the money. With ten years I'd want the people who dig the ore to own a slice of the robots. Otherwise the whole town just watches the profit fly out on the ore trains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to argue for a share scheme, where workers get shares in the automated fleet. I'd do the maintenance diploma, but slower, and save for a house deposit with Noor. And I'd use the AI tools to learn faster, like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about me, uneasy about the town. Ten years is enough for me to land somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you really think workers could own part of the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not, but some countries have funds like that for oil, so why not robots. If nobody asks, it definitely won't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a house make sense in a mine town with ten years left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the question. Probably not here, we'd buy somewhere on the coast where Noor can teach, and I'd fly in and out.

If it goes badly, the **people at the top** chose that.
think: Workers who dig the ore should **own a slice** of the robots.
Ten years is enough for him to **land somewhere**, even if the town struggles.
do: Push the union for a **share scheme** in the automated fleet.
Do the **maintenance diploma** at a slower pace.
Save a **house deposit** for somewhere on the coast.

fieldNote: His focus shifts from his own job to **who owns** the machines.
He'd buy a house **away** from the mine town, a quiet vote of no confidence.
He expects to be fine himself but **worries for the town** losing its profit.

steps.text: Push the union to argue for worker shares in the fleet
Do the maintenance diploma part-time over three years
Save a house deposit with Noor
Buy a home on the coast and fly in to the mine

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time for anyone, not even someone who likes tech. What would help is the company and government paying for real retraining and some kind of income while you do it. Every new machine on the mine came with a promise that nobody would lose out, and somebody always did.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people like me would actually be good at. I'm a trainee, but I'm good at teaching the older guys apps. Nobody's asked if that's a job.

headlineQuote: Every new machine on the mine came with a promise that nobody would lose out, and somebody always did.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old trainee** blasthole drill operator at a remote iron ore mine.
He uses **AI tools daily**, rents with his teacher girlfriend Noor and has about four months saved.
He's **pro-union** and wants workers to share in automation profits.
In slow pictures he sees **opportunity**, aiming for the autonomous drill team or maintenance work.
In **AGI by 2028** his tech edge vanishes and he pivots towards paramedic training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because nobody, even tech-savvy workers, has time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** from the company and government with an **income** while studying.
